The proposal seeks to merge two operating businesses with Tata Sons, potentially changing its regulatory classification and removing the requirement for a stock market listing. With the RBI's regulatory position, reported government intervention and an approaching Annual General Meeting adding to the uncertainty, the stakes remain high. stories.headline: Assam: Flood-hit Dhodang residents demand permanent road reconstruction in Golaghat
stories.title: Assam: Flood-hit Dhodang residents demand permanent road reconstruction in Golaghat
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: BOKAKHAT: Residents of Dhodang village in Assam's Golaghat district have renewed their demand for the permanent reconstruction of the flood-ravaged Dhodang-Budhbari road, alleging that the Public Works Department (PWD) has undertaken only superficial repair work instead of addressing the long-standing problem.
The road, which connects more than ten interior villages to National Highway 37 at Numaligarh, is repeatedly damaged by annual floods caused by the Dhansiri river.
During the monsoon, the route often remains submerged, disrupting transportation and leaving thousands of residents, including students, farmers, and patients, cut off from essential services.

Locals said that despite repeated visits by Bokakhat MLA and Assam Cabinet Minister Atul Bora to assess the flood situation over the years, the road has not been included in any comprehensive project for reconstruction as a wider, elevated, all-weather road.
They questioned why such a critical flood-prone route has not received a permanent solution despite repeated appeals.

The ongoing repair work has been taken up under the Mukhya Mantri Pakki Path Nirman Abhiyan (MMPNA) with funding under RIDF-XXXI through NABARD as part of the proposed 'Budhbari Ali to Dhodang via Budhbari Gaon' road project.
According to official documents, the sanctioned length of the Dhodang section is only 1.260 km.
Residents, however, pointed out that the road requiring restoration is nearly 5 km long.

They claimed that the allocated amount of Rs 91.82 lakh has to be shared with another road project involving the Tinisuti Moriahola Ali in Kuruabahi, leaving only a limited amount for the Dhodang stretch.
Residents alleged that the current work is merely a symbolic exercise intended to project development without providing a lasting solution.

stories.title: Rahul Gandhi creating confusion over SIR and demeaning Election Commission, says BJP

article_sentences: The Andhra Pradesh BJP has criticised Congress leader Rahul Gandhi for creating confusion in the minds of the public on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and demeaning the office of the Election Commission of India (ECI).

Addressing a media conference here on Tuesday (September 29, 2026), the party’s State spokesperson Jalli Madhusudhan said the nation expected the Leader of the Opposition to behave responsibly and provide constructive suggestions to the government, but said his recent outbursts against the constitutional office of the ECI did not befit his status.

Maintaining that the SIR was a result of proposals mooted by various parties, including the regional parties, in the past to rectify anomalies in the voters’ list, Mr. Madhusudhan asked how Mr. Gandhi could oppose it now on ‘flimsy grounds’.

The spokesperson said the Congress was bent on triggering unnecessary panic in public minds on the removal of votes, when the exercise was only about cleaning up the list by removing dead and shifted voters.
“It is now clear that the Leader of the Opposition does not want the ECI to take any proactive steps to stem the rot in the system.
It also gives rise to the suspicion that he wants to extend the rights enjoyed by the Indian citizens to the illegal immigrants too,” he said.
Mr. Madhusudhan said the BJP would continue to stand by the good policies initiated by constitutional bodies such as the ECI and enlighten the public on the merits of implementing the SIR.

article_sentences: The Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) and the Uddhav Thackeray-led Shiv Sena (UBT) will hold a joint protest march against the Election Commission of India (ECI) on October 4.
The announcement comes amid the ongoing row over Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar reagrding dissent within the poll panel.

The march will start from Mumbai’s Byculla region to the BMC headquarters in CSMT, MNS chief Raj Thackeray said on Tuesday (September 29, 2026), adding that the next step to the protest will be decided after October 4.
The distance between Byculla and BMC is around 5kms.

Days after Mr. Raj Thackeray first called for demonstrations against the ECI, the Thackeray cousins on Tuesday (September 29, 2026) appealed citizen to join the cause and raise voice against the CEC, who has been accused of rigging elections in the name of SIR.
Mr. Uddhav Thackeray pointed out that the Opposition and pressure groups are demonstrating and highlighting discrepancies in their own way.
“Congress protested on September 29, Cockroach Janta Party is doing on October 2, and we will be doing on October 4.
If there is a need we will come together,” he said.

While speaking to media persons in Dadar region, Mr. Raj Thackeray reiterated that they have been constantly raising concerns over Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) and the functioning of the Election Commission, yet it was kept unresolved.

Mr. Raj Thackeray also invited all parties to join this protest march, while extended support to the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP)‘s “Jail Bharo Andolan” protest on October 2, demanding for the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
However, the Mumbai Police have denied permission to CJP for a proposed protest on October 2 at Shivaji Park in Dadar against Mr. Kumar.

stories.headline: From omission to Asiad gold: How Shafali Verma transformed her game
stories.title: From omission to Asiad gold: How Shafali Verma transformed her game
stories.summary: In November 2024, when Shafali Verma was dropped from the India team for its ODI tour of Australia, she hid the news from her father who was hospitalised with a heart attack a few days earlier. When she finally mustered the courage to tell him, Sanjeev, who introduced her to the sport and power hitting, sat silently for a few seconds before perking up. “He told me, ‘koi baat nahi, abhi aur bhi mehnat karenge’ [don’t worry, we’ll work even harder],” Verma had told Forbes India in an earlier interview. “I believe that when the going gets tough, gardan neeche karke chupchap kaam karte jao [put your head down and keep working quietly].”Two years on, Verma’s conviction has been vindicated as she has embarked on one of the most prolific phases of her career. It started in October 2024, when the 22-year-old earned a surprise recall to the ODI side, on a stage no less than the World Cup, despite not being part of the original 15-member squad. Coming in as a replacement for injured opener Pratika Rawal at the semifinal stage, Verma delivered an all-round masterclass in the final, capping her comeback with the Player of the Match award in November 2025 and celebrating her feat with her first vacation thereafter—a trip to Bali. But that was just the beginning.In her eight-year international career, Year 2026 has been Verma’s most prolific in T20Is, the format that she has long made her own with her batting blitzkrieg. By the end of the recently concluded Asian Games in Japan’s Aichi-Nagoya, where India won gold, Verma became the year’s highest run-scorer in the format, with 863 runs from 24 matches and a strike rate (runs per 100 balls) of 162.83, the highest among those from Test-playing nations.Seven of her 21 half-centuries in T20Is have come this year, along with a 49-ball century in the Asian Games semi-final—her first in white-ball cricket. The knock made Verma the first centurion in the history of the multi-sport event, where she also finished as the leading run-scorer and the only woman player to strike at over 200.“From the time I started playing cricket and realised that T20 is my favourite format, my dream was to hit a hundred. When the moment finally arrived, and I raised my bat and helmet, bachpan se aaj tak jitna hard work kiya tha, sab yaad aa gaya [I was reminded of all the hard work I have done since my childhood],” Verma told Forbes India in an interview upon her return to India. “I have waited for this for a long time.”Also Read: The innings after the World Cup final starts from zero: Shafali VermaSECOND INNINGSAt the heart of Verma’s turnaround, a Shafali 2.0 if you will, lies a more measured approach to shot-making: Aggressive, yet patient. Her 78-ball 87 in the ODI World Cup final is a telling example, where she went 20 balls without hitting a boundary before snapping out of the streak with a six. In five of her last eight matches—in the Asia Cup and at the Asian Games—Verma, an explosive opener, batted deep into the middle overs, negotiating a field spread beyond the 30-yard circle and packed with boundary riders that limited her natural, aerial game.“In these last two tournaments, she has played past the 10th over more often than not. Now you don’t see the old Shafali where she would frequently move away from the stumps [to manufacture a shot]. There’s a sense of calmness to her game as opposed to the earlier restlessness to score,” says Mithali Raj, former India captain and now a commentator. “Once you hit that level of understanding of your game, you cannot go back to your old self, you only want to keep going up a level.”Verma learnt to play on the attack from childhood, when her father set out to mould her into an aggressive opener. Initially, her shots wouldn’t travel far, but practising with heavier, wet leather balls helped her build strength and distance. While she made her international debut in 2019, at 15, it was with her heroics at the T20 World Cup in Australia the following year—when she steered India to the final as the team’s highest run-getter—that she grabbed the headlines. Ever since, her slam-bang game received widespread admiration and served her well as well. “From 2019 till about 2021, I only used to think of sixes. And that approach worked,” she says. “But after that, I started to get out in crucial matches.”For example, Verma was dismissed for 11 in the final of the Commonwealth Games at Birmingham in 2022, a match India narrowly lost to Australia by 9 runs; for 9 in the semifinal of the T20 World Cup in 2023, where Australia once again scraped past India by 5 runs; and aggregated 97 from four matches in the 2024 edition of the tournament in Dubai, where India failed to make it beyond the group stage. “For a long time, I felt I was lagging somewhere. It was after the 2024 World Cup in Dubai that I realised what needed to be worked on,” adds Verma. Soon after, she was axed from the ODI side too.THE ALL-ROUNDERWhen a young player gets dropped from a side, says Ashwani Kumar, a former Haryana player and Verma’s childhood coach, they tend to fall into a negative spiral. Not Verma, says Kumar, who has seen Verma since the time she landed up at his off-season camp in Rohtak at age 12. “She is the type who gears up to improve and fight back on merit. It reflects her mental make-up.”Out of the national team, Verma dived right into training, played domestic cricket for Haryana to iron the creases in her batting, while also sitting for special sessions with dieticians to improve her fitness. But the reset wasn’t merely physical. While she spent hours at the nets, training herself to play along the ground instead of looking to loft every shot, she also recalibrated her mind—sometimes through sessions with sports psychologists that the HCA had assigned to her and sometimes on her own.“Even during my free time at home, I would be running scenarios in my head where I should take singles if the ball wasn’t within hitting range,” she says. “Earlier, I was quite young and I didn’t know how to control my mind—so, while I had the skills, I lacked the mindset. The first step to rectifying it was acceptance. Then, through 2025, I worked very hard on my mindset.”The ability to work the ball for singles and twos has now opened up for Verma access to the entire ground, says Raj, the highest run-scorer in women’s cricket (till Smriti Mandhana recently overtook her in the Asian Games). “She is so good from the long off to the long on region—there are hardly any shots in the area that she’s mistimed in recent times,” she says. “Along with that, when you are able to play glides to the third man or flicks on the legside, it means you have upgraded your skills with low-risk shots. That's the reason she's able to play into the middle overs and if she continues like this, we’ll perhaps see her reaching those 100s more often.”Verma’s purple patch with the bat seems to be rubbing off on her bowling as well. In a recent media roundtable, she mentioned she enjoys her bowling more than batting as “it just takes one ball to get out in batting, while, with bowling, you get a chance to come back”. If she has a growing love for bowling, her recent statistics prove that bowling, too, loves her right back. Verma grabbed two key wickets in the triumphant ODI World Cup final against South Africa—of Sune Luus and Marizane Kapp—in what was only the sixth time she had bowled in 31 ODIs she had played till then; 12 of her 22 wickets in T20Is have also come this year.TWO TO TANGOPeople who’ve seen Verma from close quarters also sense an uptick in her fielding, which earlier was lagging her batting. She says she has learnt the trick to good fielding—of enjoying it. “I’ve worked on my fitness, I’m getting good reflexes,” she adds. And it’s evident from the way she’s been able to run in the deep, and from one end to the other after every over.Raj speaks about Verma’s new-found fielding chops, as does Jonathan Batty, the head coach of Delhi Capitals (DC), the franchise Verma plays for in the WPL (Women’s Premier League). “She has now developed into a fielder whom we rely on in the deep to take the catches. She dives around as well as anyone in the field,” says Batty.The former English first-class cricketer—who has seen the batter since the inaugural season in 2023, when Verma was lapped up by the side for Rs2 crore—also speaks about how Verma, a quick learner, imbibed from Meg Lanning, former Australia captain and seven-time World Cup winner who skippered the team for the first three seasons and opened the batting with her.While they were a picture of contrasts in terms of their career phases—Verma at its start and Lanning at the fag end—“it seemed to us that Shafali very quickly started to observe how Meg went about her business. There was more accuracy and precision in the way she would go about her practice,” says Batty. Eventually, it added clarity to her decision-making in shot selection: While Plan A is always to go for the big hits, it helped Verma develop Plan B, C, Ds, what have you, to minimise risks in her game and play on for longer.In its fourth season in 2026, Verma became only the second Indian after national captain Harmanpreet Kaur, and the fourth overall, to breach the 1,000-run-mark in the tournament. (Lanning—who has left DC for the UP Warriorz in the last season—is one among the two foreign players on the list.) “Once your adrenaline gets going, it’s difficult, as a batter, to bring it down. We would see her talk to Shafali after she’d hit a ball out of the ground,” says Batty.He adds: “Their dynamics was really interesting because Meg seemed to play with more freedom around Shafali—she became a bit more Shafali-like and Shafali became a little Meg-like in the way they structured their innings. article_sentences: The Supreme Court today granted bail to a 30-year-old security guard challenging the Jharkhand High Court's refusal to grant him bail in a case arising from allegedly obscene and derogatory Facebook posts against Jharkhand Chief Minister Hemant Soren's wife, Kalpana Soren, who is a sitting MLA from Gandey.

A bench of Justice M.M. Sundresh and Justice Prasanna B. Varale observed that he has been incarcerated for over a year and the maximum sentence prescribed for the offences against him is three years imprisonment.
The Court opined that custodial interrogation is not required.
Before the Supreme Court, Uraon has argued that the High Court failed to properly consider his prolonged custody and the stage of the proceedings.
His plea states that the investigation has been completed and the chargesheet has been filed.
It further says that the prosecution's case rests on electronic evidence already in its possession and that there is no requirement for his continued custody.

The plea further contends that the High Court rejected bail solely on the seriousness of the offence, which cannot be the sole ground for denying bail and as the court must consider the overall facts and circumstances.

The petitioner has also pointed out that he was granted bail in another case arising from the same alleged incident based on a complaint by Javed Ansari, the head of the Kanke Block Coordination Committee, on February 13, 2026.
He contends that the two cases arose from the same offence and that the High Court failed to give due consideration to his custody since September 6, 2025.
The plea also points out that neither case was registered at the instance of Kalpana Soren herself.
The Supreme Court has now issued notice to the State of Jharkhand on his plea against the High Court's bail rejection.
The petitioner was represented by Advocate Rahul Shyam Bhandari.

The CJI-led bench passed the direction after taking note of the transitional arrangement explained by Additional Solicitor General (ASG) Aishwarya Bhati, under which students of Classes 7, 8 and 9 would continue studying the third language but would not have to appear for a CBSE Board examination in the subject.
"There will be no pass/failure.
There will only be an appearance certificate," observed the Supreme Court despite the Centre opposing the extension of the relaxation to Class 6 students.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta submitted that detailed discussions had taken place on the top court's earlier suggestion that the present batch of Class 6 students be given an exemption from the revised three-language formula.

The Centre's second highest law officer said the government was not in favour of extending the relaxation to Class 6 students and sought permission to implement the policy for the current academic year.

stories.headline: Apraava Energy Acquires Maharashtra Transmission Project for 3 GW PSP Evacuation
stories.title: Apraava Energy Acquires Maharashtra Transmission Project for 3 GW PSP Evacuation
stories.summary: Mumbai-based Apraava Energy, an integrated energy solutions provider, has acquired the special purpose vehicle (SPV) Raigad Power Transmission Limited to develop an intrastate transmission project across Pune and Raigad districts in Maharashtra. Apraava has a long-standing presence in Maharashtra, with over 200 MW of operational wind capacity and 70 MW of operational solar capacity. In a press release, the company said it currently operates three transmission assets comprising around 1,000 circuit kilometres (ckm) of transmission lines and 3,500 MVA of substation capacity. The project marks Apraava’s first transmission asset in Maharashtra and is aimed at enhancing grid stability and reliability by enabling reliable power supply to potential pumped storage plants (PSPs) and the evacuation of around 3 GW of power from PSPs in Raigad district. With the addition of Raigad Power Transmission Limited, Apraava now has five greenfield transmission projects under construction, which will collectively add around 1,580 ckm of transmission lines and 18,000 MVA of substation capacity. Apraava Energy Secures Project Under BOOT Model Apraava Energy was awarded the project through the tariff-based competitive bidding (TBCB) process. The project involves the development of around 400 ckm of transmission lines, including approximately 340 ckm of 765 kV lines, with the remaining comprising 400 kV and 220 kV double-circuit transmission lines. It will also include a 4,500 MVA (3×1,500 MVA) 765/400/220 kV pooling station. The project will be developed under the Build, Own, Operate and Transfer ( BOOT ) model and will provide transmission services for a 35-year concession period following commissioning. It is scheduled for completion within 24 months from the signing of the Transmission Service Agreement (TSA). In addition to strengthening Maharashtra’s power transmission infrastructure, the project is expected to create direct and indirect employment opportunities during its construction and operational phases. Commenting on the project, Rajiv Ranjan Mishra, Managing Director, Apraava Energy, said, “The Raigad Power Transmission Limited project will play an important role in strengthening Maharashtra’s transmission network and enabling the reliable integration of renewable energy. Maharashtra holds a special place in our journey, as it was here that we entered the renewable energy sector with our first wind project in 2006.” Mishra added, “As one of India’s key economic and industrial hubs, Maharashtra requires a robust and resilient transmission network to meet its growing energy needs. Apraava remains focused on expanding its transmission portfolio and building the infrastructure needed to enable India’s energy transition.”

stories.headline: Hinge is launching safety features specifically for India: CEO Jackie Jantos
stories.title: Hinge is launching safety features specifically for India: CEO Jackie Jantos
stories.summary: A year before Hinge was invented, and a few more before she was to become its CEO, Jackie Jantos met her now-husband on a dating app. She came to Hinge with a personal mission of sorts: To help the world become a little less lonely.In the 10 years that Hinge has been in India, the demography itself has shifted, she says. The first wave was built amid the hangover of matrimonial apps, where the whole family was involved; now, Indian singles are seeking more autonomy in their own love lives.However, India doesn’t behave quite like other markets, and safety remains a primary concern for singles, especially women. Hinge, which industry experts estimate has roughly 1.47 million users in India—largely concentrated in the metros—has decided to launch special security layers built for the Indian market.Jantos speaks with Forbes India to explain why, and to talk about how the app aims to build an authentic experience in the age of AI-generated responses. Edited excerpts:Also Read: The Gen that went from Z to A in a weekQ. Hinge has been in India for 10 years now. What has changed in the market over the years?We speak about Hinge as ‘designed to be deleted’, and this is really all about creating an experience for singles who are looking for love and long-term relationships on our app. Hinge has been in India now for a little over 10 years, growing organically, so we know that the product plays that role for some people already in the market.In India, what we've seen take shape over the past decade, is the desire for singles to have more agency and independence in their search for love. This means developing a relationship with someone and getting to that point of clarity and commitment together, before bringing family and parents into the conversation.Q. What are the biggest barriers to Hinge’s growth in India, considering cultural attitudes towards dating, safety, monetisation, or competition?In order to be successful on Hinge, you need to feel safe, and you need to feel able to present yourself in a very authentic way. For India specifically, we've dialled up our safety features.We have ‘face check’, a feature to ensure there is a human behind the profile being developed. Then we’ve created two new features that we’re launching first in India.One of them is the ‘wait list’, that’s intended to make sure we’re careful about how we’re curating the community of singles on Hinge. While you’re waiting to come into the community, you can spend more time developing your personalised profile and prompt responses.Unique to India, we’ve also introduced the inability to take screenshots of profiles. We already have a block list feature, which allows you, from the beginning of the journey, to block others in your life that you don’t want popping up on Hinge—colleagues, family, and so on.We’re confident that these unique features will allow singles in India to feel like they can be their most authentic selves.Also Read: Indian dating apps are swiping right on small townsQ. Hinge has built its brand around being “designed to be deleted”. How does that philosophy work when your business model depends on people continuing to use the product?We talk a lot about the free experience as sacred, because for any app in the relationship space to work, it needs to have a strong community of individuals who are sort of looking for similar things. And for us, the only ways that Hinge monetises users is through paid subscriptions and a-la-carte features like ‘boosting your profile’ or ‘sending someone a rose’. There's no other model built into it. We never have advertising on Hinge. The organic growth and the momentum behind the app continues, and we believe natural user growth brings with it natural revenue growth. So, as long as we're focussed on the end goal, we continue to see that growth, and it's been fascinating to watch organic growth in a market like India, but more generally around the world.Q. In terms of Hinge’s growth in India, what are you seeing in the user base across tier 1, 2 and 3 cities? And how does Hinge fit into a market where local dating apps are also gaining traction, particularly in smaller towns?We've been in India now for a little over 10 years, and we haven't done much to promote the app in the market, and yet we've got this slowly growing user base, mostly in some of the larger urban centres, Delhi and Mumbai. And one of the things that we know now is that the user base of daters in India today represents our third largest user base in a single country. The growth has been quite large, and it's also the second highest volume of downloads of Hinge, second only to the US right now.The Hinge user base represents around 15 million users around the world looking for love. There's enormous growth to come, and we really are just getting started.Later this month, we'll roll out marketing of the app for the very first time. We're really excited about the organic growth, but we're also really excited to see the growth that comes from more specificity of us both building a stronger product, launching specific safety features for Indian singles, and then actually marketing the product for the first time.Some features like wait lists and security tools are only India specific at the moment, and we’re banking on them to stand out from competition.Also Read: How Gen Z is rewriting the rules of brand loyaltyQ. If AI can write your profile, choose your photos, craft your opening line and even suggest your replies, how much of the person are you actually dating? What checks do you hope to put in place to counter this?There are a couple things to speak about here. First, what we see with singles around the world is that there is this growing distrust of AI generally across technology platforms, and there's also a real understanding of what sort of fake looks like in all of these platforms that we engage in daily.For Hinge, our focus is really on people presenting themselves as they are, so we have a number of systems in place to both improve who's on the platform itself, and make sure that any suspicious profiles are removed. We also encourage community members who are dating to tell us when they're interacting with a profile they suspect not to be real, so our moderation teams can follow up.We know from a lot of our research that young people are mostly using AI to get a second opinion on something. So we don't necessarily see people using AI to write for them, but when we hear from users that they're experiencing that, that's something we take really seriously and we look into.The final thing that I'll note for Hinge is the entire experience has really been built to help you move off the app and to meet someone in person. So you can only have eight chats open, and you can't ‘like’ people until you are either closing out one of those chats or progressing to meet someone in person. So, a lot of the design of our actual app is to enable more of an experience of focus and moving off of the app, than to keep you on the app in conversation with people for a long time.Q. Do you, however, feel like people are second-guessing themselves more now—thinking, “AI could give me a wittier opening line or a better comeback”? In a sense, are people turning to AI to appear smarter, funnier, or more articulate? Is that something you’re looking into?Well, I would say we're living in a period where people are feeling somewhat distrustful of technology, and there is still this resonant and deep desire to find partnership. So all of the tools that we put in place can enable people to express themselves and be authentic.We offer AI as an experience on the app in three ways: First, bolstering our trust and safety tooling, and helping us keep up with bad profiles who are increasingly sophisticated in their work. Second, we operate a recommender model that's built on trying to match you based on compatibility—matching me with someone I will be likely to like, and also acknowledging that the person matched with me is likely to like me. This classic machine learning work is essentially AI, so our models get to be improved over time with the unique signal and data that we are learning from each single on the app itself.And finally, we have a couple of tools along the way to help guide people. One of them, as an example, is prompt feedback. When you're filling out your icebreaker prompts, if you need a little bit of help, you can ask for feedback on your prompt. AI won't write the prompt for you. It can never replace the human, but it can offer you some tips and help you extract what's the best of you in the actual profile space.Q. There have been many reports on people seeking AI for companionship. Do you as a dating platform see AI companionship as a competitor to dating apps?No, not at all. I do not think AI can replace humans in a relationship. And one of the most valuable things about human relationships is unpredictability. We grow because we are in community with other people who bring themselves as we bring ourselves into the relationship. In many ways, what we see with an AI companion is an environment of AI being deeply affirming of who you are and what you believe and everything you want.Connection comes through the friction in discovering who you are, and the growth that comes from doing that with another person. And this is everything that we stand for. This is to us what finding love is all about, because you're also finding a person and you're finding yourself along that journey, and that cannot be replaced by AI.
